lesson.title: Measuring Acidity: What the pH Scale Actually Tracks
lesson.summary: The pH scale is a logarithmic measure of hydrogen ion concentration that lets biologists precisely describe how acidic or basic a solution is, from stomach acid to blood to a cell's lysosomes.
lesson.body:
The pH scale is a shorthand for describing exactly how acidic or basic a solution is, based directly on the hydrogen ion chemistry just described. Formally, pH is defined as the negative base-ten logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, written pH equals negative log base ten of the H+ concentration. Practically, this means pH is just a convenient number standing in for how many free hydrogen ions are floating around in a solution.

The logarithmic part matters more than it might first seem. Because the scale is logarithmic, each single step, from pH 5 to pH 4 for instance, represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration, not a small linear step. A solution at pH 4 has ten times more free H+ than a solution at pH 5, and one hundred times more than a solution at pH 6. This compression is necessary because the actual concentrations of H+ in biological fluids range across many orders of magnitude, from roughly 0.01 molar in stomach acid down to about 0.0000000001 molar in blood, numbers too unwieldy to compare directly without a logarithmic scale.

The scale runs from 0 to 14 under normal conditions, with 7 marking neutral, the pH of pure water at room temperature, where the autoionization reaction described earlier produces equal, very small concentrations of H+ and OH-. Solutions with a pH below 7 are acidic, meaning they have a higher concentration of H+ than pure water, and solutions above 7 are basic, or alkaline, meaning they have a lower concentration of H+ and correspondingly more OH-.

Living systems span an enormous range of this scale, each tuned to its job. Gastric juice in the human stomach sits around pH 1.5 to 3.5, acidic enough to denature dietary proteins and kill most swallowed bacteria. Blood, by contrast, is held in an extremely narrow range around pH 7.35 to 7.45, just barely basic. Digestive secretions from the pancreas that enter the small intestine push the environment there to around pH 8, basic enough to neutralize the acidic material arriving from the stomach and to activate a different set of digestive enzymes. Lysosomes, the digestive organelles inside cells, maintain an acidic interior of roughly pH 4.5 to 5 so their degradative enzymes function properly without damaging the rest of the neutral cytoplasm if they leak.

These specific pH values are not arbitrary; every enzyme has a pH range in which its three-dimensional shape, and therefore its function, is optimal, and moving far outside that range can denature the protein entirely. Pepsin, the stomach's main protein-digesting enzyme, works well only in the strongly acidic environment near pH 2 and becomes essentially inactive if it reaches the near-neutral pH of the small intestine, which is exactly why the body relies on a different enzyme, trypsin, once digestion moves further along the gut. Because even small pH swings can be so disruptive, and because ordinary metabolism constantly produces acidic or basic byproducts, organisms need a way to resist those swings. That resistance is exactly what buffers provide.
